definition: Supervised learning learns a mapping from input features to known target labels or values using labeled examples.
intuition: The model studies past cases where both the inputs and correct outcomes are available, then predicts outcomes for new cases.
example: A classifier can learn from inspection records labeled defect and non-defect, while a regressor can predict a continuous measurement such as cycle time.
caveat: Performance depends on representative data and trustworthy labels, and the evaluation split must prevent leakage from repeated units, customers, or time periods.
quality_example: Train a defect-risk classifier on historical inspection features and evaluate it on a later production period that was not used during training.

definition: Unsupervised learning finds structure in data without using a labeled target variable.
intuition: Instead of being told the correct answer, the algorithm groups, compresses, or summarizes observations according to patterns in their features.
example: Clustering can group products with similar failure signatures, and principal component analysis can reduce many correlated measurements to a smaller set of components.
caveat: Discovered groups are not automatically meaningful; domain experts must validate whether the structure supports a real decision.
quality_example: Cluster non-confidential sensor summaries to identify recurring process profiles, then ask engineers whether the clusters correspond to known operating conditions.

definition: Classification predicts one of a finite set of categories, such as pass versus fail or one defect type among several classes.
intuition: The model estimates which class is most plausible from the available features and often returns class probabilities as well as a label.
example: A binary classifier can predict whether a returned product is likely to require rework.
caveat: Accuracy can be misleading when classes are imbalanced, so precision, recall, F1-score, and the confusion matrix should also be reviewed.
quality_example: Use process settings and inspection measurements to classify a unit as pass or fail, while evaluating recall for the rare failure class.

definition: Regression predicts a continuous numerical target.
intuition: The model estimates how the expected value of an outcome changes with the input features.
example: A regression model can estimate remaining useful life, cycle time, concentration, or expected warranty cost.
caveat: Residual diagnostics and error metrics such as MAE or RMSE are needed because a single average score can hide systematic bias.
quality_example: Predict a continuous lab measurement from process variables and inspect whether residuals become larger at the high end of the measurement range.

definition: Clustering groups observations so that members of the same cluster are more similar to one another than to members of other clusters.
intuition: The algorithm creates segments from feature patterns without using a known outcome label.
example: K-means can group customers by usage behavior, while density-based methods can discover irregularly shaped groups and isolate noise points.
caveat: Results depend strongly on feature scaling, distance choice, and the selected number of clusters, and clusters require domain interpretation.
quality_example: Cluster complaint records by encoded symptoms and product families, then review whether each cluster represents a coherent failure pattern.

definition: A train-validation-test split separates data for fitting model parameters, selecting modeling choices, and estimating final generalization.
intuition: The test set acts as an untouched final exam; using it repeatedly for tuning makes the score optimistic.
example: A project can use 70 percent of records for training, 15 percent for validation, and 15 percent for final testing.
caveat: Random splitting is inappropriate when time order, repeated entities, groups, or leakage-prone records require grouped or temporal splitting.
quality_example: Train on earlier production months, tune on a later month, and reserve the newest month for the final test when the model will be used prospectively.

definition: Cross-validation repeatedly trains and evaluates a model on different folds to estimate how performance varies across subsets of the data.
intuition: Each record is used for validation in one fold and for training in the other folds, producing several performance estimates.
example: Five-fold stratified cross-validation can evaluate a classifier while preserving the class proportion in each fold.
caveat: The fold strategy must match deployment conditions; grouped or time-series cross-validation is needed when ordinary random folds would leak information.
quality_example: Use group cross-validation so records from the same customer or production lot never appear in both training and validation folds.

definition: Data leakage occurs when training or feature preparation uses information that would not be available at prediction time or information from the evaluation set.
intuition: The model appears unusually accurate because it has indirectly seen the answer or a proxy for it.
example: Fitting a scaler on the full dataset before splitting, or including a post-failure repair code as a predictor of failure, causes leakage.
caveat: Leakage can occur through time, repeated entities, target-derived features, preprocessing, labels, and manual data corrections.
quality_example: Place imputation, scaling, and feature selection inside a pipeline that is fit separately within each training fold.

definition: Overfitting occurs when a model learns training-specific noise or idiosyncrasies and performs worse on unseen data.
intuition: The model memorizes details instead of learning patterns that generalize.
example: A deep decision tree may perfectly classify training records but fail on a later production period.
caveat: A small train-validation gap does not guarantee generalization if both sets share leaked or duplicated information.
quality_example: Compare training and validation curves, use grouped validation, and simplify the model or increase regularization when validation performance deteriorates.

definition: Underfitting occurs when a model is too simple, poorly trained, or missing important features, so it performs poorly on both training and unseen data.
intuition: The model cannot capture the main relationship present in the data.
example: A straight-line model may underfit a strongly nonlinear relationship between temperature and defect risk.
caveat: Adding complexity is not the only remedy; data quality, feature representation, optimization, and label noise should also be investigated.
quality_example: If both training and validation errors remain high, add meaningful features or use a model capable of representing nonlinear effects.

definition: L1 regularization adds the absolute values of model coefficients to the loss function.
intuition: The penalty encourages some coefficients to become exactly zero, creating a sparse model.
example: Lasso regression can perform prediction while removing weak linear features.
caveat: With highly correlated predictors, L1 may select one feature somewhat arbitrarily and discard others with similar information.
quality_example: Use L1-regularized logistic regression when a sparse set of interpretable process variables is desirable, then validate stability across folds.

definition: L2 regularization adds the squared values of model coefficients to the loss function.
intuition: The penalty shrinks large coefficients smoothly instead of usually forcing them exactly to zero.
example: Ridge regression can stabilize estimates when many predictors are correlated.
caveat: Features should generally be on comparable scales so the penalty is applied fairly.
quality_example: Apply L2 regularization to reduce unstable coefficients in a model built from correlated sensor measurements.

definition: Feature engineering creates or transforms variables so that the model can represent useful domain relationships.
intuition: Raw data may not expose the pattern directly, but ratios, time windows, interactions, and aggregated histories can make the signal easier to learn.
example: Create rolling averages, elapsed-time features, interaction terms, or defect rates by product family.
caveat: Every feature must be computable at prediction time and created inside the validation process to avoid leakage.
quality_example: Create a trailing 30-day defect rate using only records available before each prediction date.

definition: Feature selection chooses a subset of available predictors to improve simplicity, stability, speed, or generalization.
intuition: Removing redundant or noisy features can make the model easier to understand and less sensitive to random variation.
example: Selection can use domain knowledge, regularization, permutation importance, or cross-validated recursive elimination.
caveat: Selection must be performed within the training folds; selecting on the full dataset leaks validation information.
quality_example: Run feature selection inside each cross-validation fold and compare whether the selected variables remain stable across folds.

definition: Standardization transforms a feature by subtracting its mean and dividing by its standard deviation.
intuition: The transformed feature is centered near zero and measured in standard-deviation units.
example: Standardization helps distance-based models, linear models with regularization, and neural networks when features use very different units.
caveat: The mean and standard deviation must be learned from the training data only and then applied unchanged to validation and test data.
quality_example: Fit StandardScaler inside a scikit-learn pipeline so production measurements are scaled with training statistics.

definition: Normalization rescales values to a chosen range or norm, such as mapping a feature to zero through one or scaling a vector to unit length.
intuition: It changes magnitude while preserving a relative pattern defined by the selected normalization rule.
example: Min-max scaling maps the training minimum to zero and training maximum to one.
caveat: Min-max normalization is sensitive to outliers and future values may fall outside the original range.
quality_example: Normalize bounded sensor features only after checking for extreme values and fit the transformation on the training period.

definition: Missing-value handling addresses absent observations through deletion, imputation, explicit missing indicators, or models that support missingness.
intuition: A blank value can mean random loss, a systematic process condition, or that a measurement was not applicable.
example: Median imputation can be combined with a binary indicator showing that the original value was missing.
caveat: Imputation must be learned from training data, and missingness itself may change after deployment.
quality_example: Track missing-rate trends by instrument and include a missing indicator when absence may reflect a process issue.

definition: Outliers are observations that differ substantially from the main data pattern.
intuition: An extreme value may be a valid rare event, a measurement error, a data-entry problem, or evidence of a new process condition.
example: A sensor reading far outside its historical range should be investigated before being removed.
caveat: Automatic deletion can erase the very failures a quality model is intended to detect.
quality_example: Flag extreme measurements for review, verify the measurement system, and compare robust and non-robust models before deciding how to handle them.

definition: Class imbalance occurs when one class is much rarer than another.
intuition: A model can achieve high accuracy by mostly predicting the majority class while missing the events that matter.
example: If only one percent of units fail, a classifier that predicts pass for every unit has 99 percent accuracy but zero failure recall.
caveat: Resampling and class weights must be applied only to training data, and evaluation should reflect real deployment prevalence.
quality_example: Use precision-recall curves and class-weighted training to evaluate rare-defect detection.

definition: Precision is the fraction of predicted positive cases that are truly positive: TP divided by TP plus FP.
intuition: It answers, 'When the model raises an alert, how often is the alert correct?'
example: High precision reduces unnecessary inspections caused by false alarms.
caveat: Precision depends on the classification threshold and the prevalence of the positive class.
quality_example: Use precision when false defect alerts are costly because they trigger expensive manual investigation.

definition: Recall is the fraction of actual positive cases that the model identifies: TP divided by TP plus FN.
intuition: It answers, 'Of all real positive cases, how many did the model catch?'
example: High recall is important when missing a true safety or quality failure is costly.
caveat: Increasing recall often lowers precision, so the threshold should reflect business costs and capacity.
quality_example: Prioritize recall when the main goal is to capture as many true failures as possible for follow-up.

definition: F1-score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall.
intuition: It becomes high only when both precision and recall are reasonably high.
example: F1-score is useful for comparing classifiers on an imbalanced dataset when precision and recall are both important.
caveat: It ignores true negatives and does not encode the actual cost of false positives versus false negatives.
quality_example: Report F1 together with the confusion matrix and class prevalence rather than using it as the only success measure.

definition: ROC-AUC measures how well a scoring model ranks positive cases above negative cases across classification thresholds.
intuition: It is the probability that a randomly selected positive case receives a higher score than a randomly selected negative case.
example: An ROC-AUC of 0.5 indicates random ranking, while higher values indicate better discrimination.
caveat: ROC-AUC can look strong on highly imbalanced data even when precision for the rare class is poor.
quality_example: Use ROC-AUC for overall ranking ability but also review precision-recall performance for rare defects.

definition: PR-AUC summarizes the precision-recall trade-off across thresholds.
intuition: It focuses on performance for the positive class and is especially informative when positives are rare.
example: A defect detector can be compared using the area under its precision-recall curve.
caveat: PR-AUC depends on positive-class prevalence, so values from datasets with different prevalence are not directly comparable.
quality_example: Use PR-AUC to compare rare-failure models evaluated on the same representative test population.

definition: A confusion matrix counts true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives.
intuition: It shows which kinds of classification mistakes the model makes instead of reducing performance to one number.
example: The matrix can reveal that a model catches most failures but generates many false alarms.
caveat: Counts should be interpreted with class prevalence and, when relevant, normalized rates and business costs.
quality_example: Review confusion matrices at the chosen operating threshold for each product family to detect uneven performance.

definition: Mean absolute error is the average absolute difference between predicted and observed numerical values.
intuition: It expresses a typical error in the same units as the target.
example: An MAE of two hours means predictions differ from actual cycle time by two hours on average.
caveat: MAE treats all absolute errors linearly and can hide whether errors are systematically positive or negative.
quality_example: Use MAE to communicate average prediction error for a continuous process measurement in its original units.

definition: Root mean squared error is the square root of the average squared prediction error.
intuition: Squaring gives larger errors more influence, so RMSE penalizes occasional large misses more than MAE.
example: RMSE is useful when large prediction errors are especially costly.
caveat: It is sensitive to outliers and should be compared with MAE and residual plots.
quality_example: Compare RMSE and MAE for a cycle-time model to determine whether a small number of large errors dominate performance.

definition: R-squared is the proportion of target variance explained by a regression model relative to predicting the target mean.
intuition: It compares the model's squared error with a simple mean baseline.
example: An R-squared of 0.70 means the model explains 70 percent of the variance in the evaluated data under that definition.
caveat: A high R-squared does not prove causality, unbiased predictions, or good performance on future data.
quality_example: Report R-squared with MAE, RMSE, residual diagnostics, and a time-appropriate test set.

definition: Logistic regression models the log-odds of a class as a linear combination of input features and converts the result to a probability.
intuition: Each coefficient changes the log-odds while the sigmoid function keeps the predicted probability between zero and one.
example: It can estimate the probability that a unit fails inspection from process measurements.
caveat: The linear log-odds assumption may be too restrictive without transformations or interactions, and probabilities may need calibration.
quality_example: Use regularized logistic regression as an interpretable baseline for defect-risk prediction.

definition: Linear regression predicts a continuous outcome as a weighted sum of input features plus an intercept.
intuition: Each coefficient represents an expected change in the target for a one-unit feature change while other included features are held constant.
example: It can estimate cycle time from workload and process settings.
caveat: Interpretation depends on assumptions, feature specification, correlated predictors, and whether the data support a causal claim.
quality_example: Inspect residuals and influential points before using a linear model to explain variation in a process measurement.

definition: A decision tree recursively splits the feature space into regions and predicts from the observations in each terminal leaf.
intuition: It behaves like a sequence of if-then questions.
example: A tree may first split on temperature, then on pressure, to estimate failure risk.
caveat: Deep trees can overfit and small data changes can produce a different tree.
quality_example: Limit depth and leaf size, then validate the tree on a later production period.

definition: A random forest averages many decision trees trained on bootstrap samples and random subsets of features.
intuition: Individual trees are noisy, but averaging decorrelated trees reduces variance.
example: A random forest can model nonlinear interactions in defect-risk data without extensive manual feature transformations.
caveat: Feature importance can be biased or misleading, and probability estimates may require calibration.
quality_example: Use permutation importance on held-out data to investigate which process variables support a random-forest defect model.

definition: Gradient boosting builds an additive sequence of weak learners, with each new learner focusing on errors left by the current ensemble.
intuition: The model improves step by step by correcting residual mistakes.
example: Boosted trees often perform well on structured tabular data with nonlinear relationships.
caveat: Learning rate, tree depth, number of estimators, and leakage-safe validation require careful tuning.
quality_example: Tune a boosted-tree model with grouped cross-validation when several records come from the same production lot.

definition: A neural network composes layers of weighted transformations and nonlinear activation functions to learn complex mappings.
intuition: Each layer builds a new representation from the previous layer, allowing the model to capture interactions and nonlinear patterns.
example: A feed-forward network can predict a continuous target from many sensor features.
caveat: Neural networks can require more data and tuning than simpler models and may be difficult to interpret.
quality_example: Compare a neural network with a simpler baseline and monitor validation performance rather than assuming greater complexity is better.

definition: A convolutional neural network uses learnable filters that scan local regions and share weights across positions.
intuition: The same pattern detector can recognize an edge or texture wherever it appears in an image.
example: A CNN can classify surface defects in product images.
caveat: Performance can fail under changes in lighting, camera position, background, or product appearance.
quality_example: Evaluate defect-image performance across production lines and lighting conditions, not only on random image splits.

definition: A recurrent neural network processes a sequence while carrying a hidden state from earlier steps.
intuition: The current representation depends on both the current input and information accumulated from the past.
example: An RNN can process time-ordered sensor readings or token sequences.
caveat: Basic RNNs can struggle with long-range dependencies because gradients may vanish or explode.
quality_example: Use a sequence-aware split when evaluating an RNN on time-ordered process data.

definition: An LSTM is a recurrent architecture with gates that control what information is stored, forgotten, and exposed.
intuition: The gates help preserve useful information over longer sequences than a basic RNN.
example: An LSTM can model temporal patterns in equipment measurements.
caveat: LSTMs are sequential and can be slower to train than parallel Transformer architectures.
quality_example: Compare an LSTM with lag-feature baselines and evaluate it on future time windows.

definition: A Transformer represents sequences mainly through attention and position information rather than recurrent state updates.
intuition: Each token can directly combine information from other relevant tokens, enabling parallel processing during training.
example: Transformers support language generation, translation, document search, vision models, and multimodal systems.
caveat: Attention cost can grow quickly with sequence length, and strong language generation does not guarantee factual correctness.
quality_example: Use a Transformer to summarize non-confidential technical text, then evaluate faithfulness and require human review.

definition: Attention computes weighted combinations of value vectors, where weights are derived from the compatibility of queries and keys.
intuition: The model decides which other positions are most useful for representing the current position.
example: In a sentence, a token can attend strongly to earlier words that clarify its meaning.
caveat: Attention weights are not automatically faithful explanations of a model's decision.
quality_example: Use attention-based models for long technical sequences but validate outputs with task-specific metrics and factual review.

definition: Embeddings are dense numerical vectors learned or constructed to represent items such as words, documents, products, or categories.
intuition: Items with similar usage or meaning tend to have nearby vectors in the embedding space.
example: Sentence embeddings can support semantic search by comparing vector similarity.
caveat: Similarity reflects the training objective and data, may encode bias, and is not the same as factual equivalence.
quality_example: Embed issue descriptions for retrieval, then evaluate whether nearest neighbors are useful to quality engineers.

definition: LoRA adapts a pretrained model by learning small low-rank update matrices for selected weight layers while keeping the base weights frozen.
intuition: Instead of changing every parameter, LoRA learns a compact correction that specializes the model.
example: A FLAN-T5 model can be adapted to ML education by training LoRA modules on instruction-response pairs.
caveat: A small adapter cannot compensate for poor training data, and LoRA quality still requires held-out evaluation and human review.
quality_example: Train a LoRA adapter on curated technical explanations and compare it with the unchanged base model on the same benchmark.

definition: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts a pretrained model by training a small subset of parameters or added modules.
intuition: The method reduces memory, storage, and training cost while preserving most pretrained weights.
example: LoRA, adapters, and prompt tuning are PEFT approaches.
caveat: Different tasks and architectures may require different target modules and capacity, and PEFT is not automatically better than full fine-tuning.
quality_example: Store a small adapter per technical domain while sharing the same base model.

definition: Full fine-tuning updates all or most parameters of a pretrained model on task-specific data.
intuition: The entire model can adapt, providing high capacity but requiring more memory, storage, and careful regularization.
example: A large labeled corpus can be used to update every layer of a language model.
caveat: Full fine-tuning can be expensive, overfit small datasets, and create a separate large checkpoint for each task.
quality_example: Use full fine-tuning only when the data volume, compute budget, and expected gains justify it compared with PEFT.

definition: Prompt engineering designs instructions, context, examples, and output constraints to guide a model's behavior without changing its weights.
intuition: Clear task framing reduces ambiguity and makes desired structure explicit.
example: A prompt can request a definition, one example, and one limitation in separate sections.
caveat: Prompt improvements do not guarantee factuality and can be brittle across models or domains.
quality_example: Use a fixed prompt template for technical explanations and evaluate whether it improves adherence on held-out questions.

definition: Model deployment makes a trained model available for reliable inference in an application or service.
intuition: Deployment connects model artifacts, preprocessing, inputs, outputs, monitoring, and user interaction.
example: A Gradio app can load a base model and LoRA adapter from Hugging Face and answer educational questions.
caveat: The deployed pipeline must match training preprocessing and handle latency, resource limits, failures, privacy, and model versioning.
quality_example: Deploy the reviewed adapter only after confirming that the app reports adapter mode rather than base-model fallback.

definition: Model monitoring tracks input data, predictions, latency, errors, and performance after deployment.
intuition: A model can become less useful when the operating environment changes even if the code still runs.
example: A dashboard can track prediction distributions, missing rates, alert volume, and delayed ground-truth performance.
caveat: Some outcomes arrive late or are selectively observed, so monitoring requires carefully defined proxies and retraining triggers.
quality_example: Monitor defect-model recall by product family when verified inspection outcomes become available.

definition: Data drift is a change in the distribution of model inputs over time.
intuition: The model sees different feature values or populations than it saw during training.
example: A sensor upgrade can shift the scale of measurements even if the relationship with failure remains unchanged.
caveat: Drift does not always reduce performance, but it should trigger investigation and comparison with outcome metrics.
quality_example: Compare current and training-period feature distributions and review whether a process or measurement-system change explains the shift.

definition: Concept drift is a change in the relationship between inputs and the target outcome.
intuition: The same feature pattern may correspond to a different result after a process, policy, product, or environment changes.
example: A new manufacturing method may alter which settings predict defects.
caveat: Concept drift generally requires labeled outcomes to confirm and may be confused with data drift or label changes.
quality_example: Track performance over time and retrain when the mapping from process features to verified failures changes.

definition: Probability calibration measures whether predicted probabilities match observed event frequencies.
intuition: Among cases assigned a probability near 0.8, approximately 80 percent should be positive in a well-calibrated model.
example: Reliability diagrams and Brier scores can assess calibration.
caveat: A model can rank cases well but still be poorly calibrated, and calibration can change when prevalence changes.
quality_example: Calibrate a defect-risk model on a validation period before using probabilities to allocate inspection capacity.

definition: Model explainability uses methods and documentation to help people understand model behavior, important features, and individual predictions.
intuition: Explanations provide evidence about how a model uses information, but they do not prove causality or correctness.
example: Permutation importance can summarize global dependence, while SHAP values can describe contributions for one prediction.
caveat: Explanations can be unstable, correlated features can share credit, and users may over-trust visually persuasive outputs.
quality_example: Combine global and local explanations with domain review before changing a quality process.

definition: A data pipeline reliably moves and transforms data from sources into analysis, training, or inference-ready datasets.
intuition: The pipeline makes data preparation repeatable instead of relying on manual one-off steps.
example: A pipeline can validate schemas, clean records, create features, and write versioned datasets.
caveat: Silent schema changes, duplicate records, late-arriving data, and inconsistent training-serving logic can invalidate results.
quality_example: Add checks for duplicate case IDs, missing fields, and unexpected product categories before producing a monthly quality dataset.

definition: MLOps applies software engineering, data management, automation, testing, versioning, deployment, and monitoring practices to machine-learning systems.
intuition: A model is treated as one component of a reproducible product lifecycle rather than as a notebook-only experiment.
example: A workflow can version data and models, run tests in CI, deploy a reviewed artifact, and monitor production behavior.
caveat: More tooling is not automatically better; controls should match the system's risk, scale, and maintenance needs.
quality_example: Store experiment metadata, tests, model cards, release manifests, and monitoring definitions for a quality-assistant project.

definition: Quality analytics classification predicts a discrete quality outcome such as pass, fail, defect type, or escalation category.
intuition: Historical labeled records are used to estimate the class of a new unit, case, or event.
example: Predict whether a complaint is likely to require engineering escalation from non-confidential structured features.
caveat: Labels may reflect inconsistent human decisions, and repeated customers or products must be separated during validation.
quality_example: Evaluate recall for true escalations and review false positives with process owners.

definition: Quality analytics regression predicts a continuous quality-related quantity.
intuition: The model estimates a numerical outcome rather than assigning a class.
example: Predict expected resolution time or a continuous measurement from process and product features.
caveat: Large errors may be concentrated in certain product families, so aggregate MAE should be complemented by subgroup analysis.
quality_example: Report MAE and RMSE by product family and time period before using the prediction operationally.

definition: Quality analytics anomaly detection identifies observations that differ from expected historical patterns.
intuition: The method highlights unusual combinations or sequences for investigation without necessarily knowing every failure label.
example: Flag an uncommon combination of sensor readings or a sudden increase in complaint volume.
caveat: An anomaly is not automatically a defect; thresholds and alerts require domain review and capacity planning.
quality_example: Route high-scoring anomalies to engineers and track how often reviewed alerts correspond to actionable issues.
